Unlike many African xylophones it has no gourd resonators and produces no buzzing timbre; in orchestral usage the xylophone has a higher range than the marimba and a drier tone. Volume and hardness can be adjusted with the material of the beater: hard rubber and acrylic are brighter, medium rubber or yarn softer, and wooden beaters lighter and gentler. Three players play fast in interlocking rhythm, which makes the sound short and strongly rhythmic.

In listening, notice the three-player line-up: two face each other and strike the same set of twelve logs in a fast interlocking way. The instrument has no resonating gourds and none of the buzzing timbre common to other African xylophones.
阿馬丁達木琴源自今烏干達布干達，屬木琴類。關於木琴起源，Nettl 提出約公元5: The amadinda comes from Buganda in what is now Uganda and belongs to the xylophone class. On the origin of the xylophone, Nettl proposed that it came from Southeast Asia to Africa around AD 500, while Roger Blench argues for independent African development. The amadinda's form differs from many African xylophones: it is made of twelve bars tuned to a pentatonic scale, uses no gourd resonators and produces no buzzing; it is usually played by three people, two facing each other and striking the bars in a fast interlocking technique.
阿馬丁達木琴（Amadinda）是源自烏干達布干達的木琴類定音體鳴樂器，H-S: The amadinda is a tuned idiophone of the xylophone class from Buganda in Uganda, H-S number 111.212. It is made of twelve logs tuned to a pentatonic scale, has no gourd resonators, and does not produce the buzzing timbre common to other African xylophones. It is usually played by three people, two of them facing each other and striking the same row of logs in a fast interlocking technique. The instrument is associated with the Buganda region and belongs to the xylophone family.

It is played by striking the keys with beaters, usually by three people, two of them sitting face to face and alternately striking the same set of keys in a fast interlocking technique. The beginner's first task is to learn the layout of the keys and where the pentatonic scale lies, then to practise a steady two-handed stroke, and finally to fit in with another player's rhythm and keep a fast interlocking part going.
